title: Linking vulnerability and resilience for climate change adaptation: a GeoAI-integrated assessment across Europe
abstract: Climate change is reshaping key ecological processes such as drought cycles, heat stress, disturbance regimes, and air quality regulation. These changes generate cascading impacts on ecosystems and the human societies that depend on them. There is therefore a pressing need for frameworks that not only map where adaptation is required but also explain why these needs arise. Existing approaches often remain limited: top-down climate scenarios overlook local stressors, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) applications suffer from subjectivity, and machine learning models frequently lack interpretability. To address these limitations, this study introduces an integrated framework that combines ecological, climatic, and socio-economic indicators with MCDM, Geographic Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), and explainable machine learning to provide spatial mapping and a sensitivity-based interpretation of adaptation needs. A Climate Change Adaptation Index (CCAI) was constructed for 1,187 NUTS-3 regions using 44 indicators of vulnerability and resilience, including land surface temperature, burned areas, hydrological stress, demographic sensitivity, renewable energy use, and institutional effectiveness. Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (F-AHP) was employed to derive factor weights, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to analyse indicator interactions. The findings highlight three major discoveries: (i) heat stress, precipitation, and renewable energy share emerge as the dominant ecological and socio-economic contributors to variation in the constructed index; (ii) Southern and Mediterranean Europe exhibit significantly higher adaptation requirements than Northern Europe, reflecting marked spatial disparities; and (iii) SHAP-based explainability uncovers regional heterogeneity by showing how indicator effects vary across contexts, thereby extending expert-based weighting results with data-driven sensitivity evidence within the constructed index. By linking ecological processes with socio-economic conditions and supporting the analysis with interpretable machine learning, this study advances an interpretable understanding of index-based regional climate adaptation needs. The framework combines MCDM, GeoAI, and SHAP to provide transparent evidence of both global and local contributors to variation in the constructed adaptation-needs. Moving beyond descriptive spatial distributions, the framework clarifies how indicator contributions and their combinations shape the constructed CCAI scores and associated adaptation-needs patterns, enhances transparency, and provides actionable insights for policymakers. The approach is scalable and policy-relevant, supporting targeted strategies to strengthen Europe’s climate resilience.
problem: Existing climate adaptation approaches are limited, as top-down scenarios overlook local stressors, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) is subjective, and machine learning models lack interpretability, thus failing to provide a unified, transparent assessment of vulnerability and resilience.
method: The study introduces an integrated framework combining multi-criteria decision-making, Geographic Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), and explainable machine learning (SHAP) to construct a Climate Change Adaptation Index that assesses regional adaptation needs across Europe by linking vulnerability and resilience indicators.
task: The task is to introduce an integrated framework combining MCDM, GeoAI, and explainable machine learning to spatially map and interpret climate change adaptation needs across Europe based on ecological, climatic, and socio-economic indicators.
innovation: This paper introduces an integrated framework combining multi-criteria decision-making, GeoAI, and explainable machine learning to assess climate adaptation needs across Europe, providing transparent, data-driven insights into the ecological and socio-economic drivers that shape vulnerability and resilience.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Although global frameworks emphasize broad drivers of climate risk (UNDRR 2015; UNFCCC 2015), translation into ecological process-based regional analysis remains limited. Composite indices and decision-support tools are widely used to simplify complexity into measurable forms, but their potential to reflect ecological processes has not been fully realized (IPCC 2022; ND-GAIN 2024; Ustaoglu et al. 2024). Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) provides a robust framework for integrating ecological and socio-economic factors into climate adaptation assessment, yet it often requires simplifications that reduce its ability to represent dynamic ecological processes (Croeser et al. 2021; Lamichhane et al. 2022). Moreover, existing applications frequently concentrate only on vulnerability or risk, leaving the interplay between vulnerability and resilience insufficiently explored at a regional scale. This gap underscores the need for frameworks that simultaneously address both ecological vulnerabilities and socio-economic resilience capacities.

The analysis was conducted for Mediterranean (IT, ES, PT, EL, MT) and Northern Europe (NO, SE, FI, DK, IE, EE, LV, LT) representing groups with the highest and lowest constructed CCAI levels. The results indicate that Mediterranean regions are driven more strongly by vulnerability (61.5%), whereas Northern Europe shows a greater share of resilience (45.9%) indicators within the constructed SHAP-based decomposition. This contrast demonstrates that adaptation differences across Europe are not only about where index-based requirements are concentrated but also about how vulnerability and resilience components combine in the constructed CCAI. For the Mediterranean, vulnerability is dominated by LST, Net Migration, and Seismic Risk; while for Northern Europe resilience is primarily associated with Annual Precipitation, Renewable Energy Share and Disaster Risk Reduction implementation.

Based on the CCAI results, a thematic map illustrating the levels of climate adaptation requirements across the study area was produced, as presented in Fig. 3. The CCAI values were classified into five categories—very low, low, moderate, high, and very high—using the Natural Breaks (Jenks’ optimization) method in the GIS environment. This classification reduces the average deviation within classes while maximizing differences between class means. The results suggest that regions in Southern Europe including Spain, Italy, Greece, and parts of the Southern Balkans show high adaptation needs driven by heat and extremes.
